question:
A risk analyst at a Canadian pension plan is completing Step 5 of an MDS. The scenario’s policy and implied nonpolicy shocks and the portfolio positions are below (CAD millions):

| Position | Driver | Exposure | Shock (%) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Equity index futures | Equity index (policy) | 40 | −6 |
| Bond portfolio | Bond index (implied) | 25 | 2 |

The plan also holds put options on the equity index. Under the scenario shocks, a delta (linear) approximation gives a P&L of +1.1 on the puts, and a full revaluation gives +1.6. The scenario z-score is 2.4. Returns on the futures and bonds are linear in the shocks. What is the best estimate of the portfolio stress-test P&L?

options.A: CAD −1.9 million
options.B: CAD −1.3 million
options.C: CAD −0.3 million
options.D: CAD −0.8 million

solution:
Canadian pension Step 5 P&L with linear positions plus equity puts; best estimate.

**Concept and theory**

Step 5 turns the full perturbation vector into a P&L. For positions whose returns are linear in the factor shocks, P&L is exposure times shock, summed across factors:

P&L $= \sum_{\text{j}} \text{E}_{\text{j}} \text{r}_{\text{j}}$,

where $\text{E}_{\text{j}}$ is the position’s exposure to factor j (here in CAD millions per unit return) and $\text{r}_{\text{j}}$ is the shock to factor j from the full (policy and implied nonpolicy) perturbation vector. Positions with embedded optionality have nonlinear payoffs, so a linear (delta) approximation misstates their P&L under large shocks. question:
The CRO of Bank Alpha is reviewing a report from the US Federal Reserve on the recent supervisory stress test performed on Bank Alpha. The report notes that while Bank Alpha continues to build its capital levels and strengthen its ability to lend during periods of stressed market conditions, the bank’s recent acquisition of a large regional competitor and its growing exposure to digital assets make it vulnerable under “severely adverse” scenarios. After discussing the stress test report, Bank Alpha’s board of directors asks the CRO to critically review the bank’s risk management practices. A summary of the CRO’s findings is given below:

- Item 1: Bank Alpha applies a counterparty’s marginal default probability and the correlation of its own credit spread with the counterparty’s credit spread as key inputs in stress testing counterparty credit risk.
- Item 2: Bank Alpha incorporates scenario analysis in its capital planning process but only considers scenarios that lead to the quantification of risk.
- Item 3: Bank Alpha considers that contingency funding planning stress scenarios are independent of its liquidity stress scenarios.
- Item 4: Bank Alpha complies with the regulatory requirement in sharing information about cybersecurity threats with peer banks to enable regulators effectively monitor and mitigate systemic risk. Which of the findings reported by the CRO in relation to Bank Alpha’s stress testing and scenario analysis is aligned with best practices?

options.A: Item 1
options.B: Item 2
options.C: Item 3
options.D: Item 4

solution:
**Concept**

A best-practice check across four frameworks: stress testing counterparty credit risk (include one’s own default and the correlation between the two credit spreads), stress testing within the risk appetite framework, alignment of contingency funding plan scenarios with liquidity stress scenarios, and cyber-threat information sharing.

**Exam trap.** Option D turns a recommendation into a requirement. Sharing cyber-threat information between banks is voluntary in most jurisdictions; regulators facilitate it.

**Note.** The LO printed in the 2026 exam is worded slightly differently from the Master LO Map; mapped to the closest map LO.

**Learning objectives tested:** CR-21e, ORR-7a, LTR-11a, ORR-8d.

question: A senior risk analyst at a Canadian regional bank is presenting to newly hired analysts on why broad-based supervisory stress testing became the regulators’ main tool for assessing bank capital adequacy during the 2007 to 2009 financial crisis. Which of the following statements should she include as most accurate?

options.A: Firms such as Lehman and Wachovia were adequately or even well capitalized under the regulatory capital rules disclosed in their filings before they failed or nearly failed, so published capital ratios lost credibility.
options.B: Stress testing was adopted because it answers a different question from regulatory and internal economic capital models, which do not seek the capital needed to support a bank’s risk taking.
options.C: Stress testing was favored because bank balance sheets are highly transparent, so supervisors could verify each bank’s results quickly from its public filings and existing reports.
options.D: Supervisory stress tests were designed to guarantee that no participating bank would fail, a goal that regulatory and economic capital models had never been calibrated to achieve.

solution:
Stem summary: Canadian bank analyst explaining to new hires why supervisory stress testing became the crisis capital tool.

**Concept and theory**

Schuermann opens with a simple taxonomy: there are three kinds of capital (and liquidity): (1) what the bank has, (2) what the bank needs to support its business activities, and (3) what the regulators think it needs. Regulatory capital rules, bank-internal “economic capital” models and stress tests all try to answer the same question: how much capital and liquidity is needed to support the institution’s risk taking. Capital adequacy concerns the right side of the balance sheet (net worth); liquidity concerns the left side (the share of liquid assets).

question: An internal auditor at an Australian bank is reviewing the 2009 Supervisory Capital Assessment Program (SCAP) as a case study for the bank’s AUD capital planning manual. She notes that a successful macro-prudential stress testing program in a crisis has two components. All US bank holding companies with assets above \$100 billion at year-end 2008 took part. Which of the following best describes how the SCAP delivered both components?

options.A: Banks’ internal economic capital models sized the capital hole, and the hole was filled by requiring the Federal Reserve to buy preferred shares in every participating bank.
options.B: A supervisory loss assessment under a stressful macro scenario sized the hole, and the Treasury’s Capital Assistance Program filled it by injecting equity into all participating banks.
options.C: A supervisory loss assessment under a stressful macro scenario sized the hole, and the Treasury’s Capital Assistance Program stood ready as a credible backstop that no bank needed to draw on.
options.D: A supervisory loss assessment under a stressful macro scenario sized the hole, and the backstop was credible because the participating banks, not the Treasury, were the strongest debt issuers.

solution:
Stem summary: Australian auditor reviewing how the 2009 SCAP sized and filled the capital hole.

**Concept and theory**

GARP states that a successful macro-prudential stress testing program, particularly in a crisis, has at least two components:

1. a credible assessment of the capital strength of the tested institutions, to size the capital “hole” that needs to be filled; and
2. a credible way of filling that hole.

The 2009 US SCAP is the worked example. The US entered 2009 with enormous uncertainty about its banks. Investors would not commit capital, partly because of the threat of later government dilution. question: A regulator at a national supervisory agency is presenting to newly hired bank examiners on how the US Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review (CCAR), in operation since 2011, changed scenario specification relative to the 2009 SCAP. Which of the following statements best describes the change and its purpose?

options.A: CCAR replaced the common supervisory scenario with bank-designed scenarios, because supervisors no longer needed to compare banks’ results under one scenario.
options.B: CCAR asked banks to submit results under their own baseline and stress scenarios in addition to the common scenario, revealing bank-specific and possibly common risks.
options.C: CCAR asked banks to submit results under their own stress scenarios, which helped microprudential supervision but by design gave supervisors no macro-prudential insight.
options.D: CCAR required supervisors to design a separate stress scenario for each bank, tailored to that bank’s business mix and geographic footprint, in place of one common scenario.

Until CCAR, every supervisory stress test imposed the same scenario on all banks. Any scenario is more severe for some banks than others depending on business mix and geographic footprint. GARP compares this one-size-fits-all approach with regulatory vs. economic capital: regulatory capital is the same for all banks by design, while economic capital reflects each bank’s own business mix. The problem becomes acute in normal times, when there is more debate about what a relevant adverse scenario looks like.

III. The real difficulty in scenario design is specifying a coherent joint outcome of all relevant risk factors, because when one factor moves significantly the others move too.

question:
A risk consultant is presenting on the evolution of macro-prudential stress testing requirements established in response to the global financial crisis of 2007 – 2009. The consultant compares features of the following three stress tests:

- The 2009 Supervisory Capital Assessment Program (SCAP) test
- The 2011 European Banking Association (EBA) test
- The 2012 Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review (CCAR) test

Which of the following elements of these stress tests or their resulting impacts is correct for the analyst to include in the presentation?

options.A: Several Spanish banks failed the EBA stress test, and Spain imposed stricter countrywide stress tests the following year that resulted in some banks raising capital.
options.B: The SCAP stress test scenario was less severe compared to later US stress tests and did not result in any increased capital requirements for participating banks.
options.C: The CCAR test required banks to evaluate both a base case and a stress scenario, while the EBA test only included a stress scenario.
options.D: The SCAP test only disclosed overall loss rates for retail and commercial exposures, while the EBA test expanded disclosure to individual geographical regions and asset classes.

solution:
**Concept**

Evolution of stress tests. SCAP (US, 2009): a single stress scenario, with bank-level results by asset class published; ten banks had to raise USD 75 billion. CCAR (US, from 2011): annual, linked to capital plans. EBA (Europe, 2011): base and stress scenarios, with detailed disclosure, followed by further tests in Spain.

**Exam trap.** Each wrong option swaps a feature between the three exercises. SCAP did lead to capital raising and did disclose loss rates by asset class.
